title: What Are Authentic Materials?
brief: Define authentic materials using the source's own definition: materials used in the target culture for actual communicative needs, enabling learners to hear, read, and produce language as it is used in that culture. Introduce the four categories the source identifies—realia (objects), printed texts, images, and multimedia—and give two or three concrete examples from each category as listed in the source (e.g., menus, maps, brochures, radio programs, video, schedules, advertisements). Distinguish authentic materials from authentic tasks, using the source's definition of authentic tasks as activities used in the real world for actual communication needs. Close by noting that textbooks increasingly include authentic materials but that teachers also use them to supplement the textbook.

title: Why Authentic Materials Motivate Learners
brief: Draw exclusively on the source's five stated reasons for using authentic materials in the classroom: they reflect real language use in culturally appropriate contexts; they are interesting and motivating; they can be chosen according to learner interests or needs, or chosen by learners themselves; they help learners develop survival language skills; and they build tolerance for what learners cannot yet understand so they can extract maximum meaning from what they do understand. Illustrate each reason with the source's own examples where available—for instance, the show-and-tell realia activity in which older students conveyed pride in completing the task, or the kindergarten children who began participating with enthusiasm once the dolls were introduced. Do not cite any research; ground every claim in the source text.

title: Grading the Task, Not the Text
brief: Explain the core principle that teachers adapt the activity or task to suit learner level rather than simplifying the authentic text itself. Use the source's guidelines for choosing materials—appropriate for the learner age group and proficiency level, containing examples of the lesson point, in a style of English learners are likely to hear and use—to show how the same material can serve different levels depending on what students are asked to do with it. Draw on the source's observation that image-heavy activities such as the Washington D.C. trip-planning task 'could be used with almost any age and proficiency level, because it depends heavily on pictures,' and that the hometown poster activity 'could be adapted to any age or proficiency level.' Emphasise that the teacher's role is to design authentic-like tasks that match learner readiness, not to rewrite the source text.

title: Real-World Materials Across Levels: Source Examples
brief: Walk through the source's concrete classroom examples to show how menus, schedules, maps, brochures, magazines, newspapers, and broadcasts are matched to different proficiency levels through task design. Cover the four video-segment examples in the source's answer key: the kindergarten realia lesson (dolls and clothing, beginner vocabulary); the show-and-tell items with 8–10-year-olds at high-beginner level; the intermediate integrated-skills tasks using wall maps, magazine pictures, and brochures for trip planning and hometown posters; and the high-intermediate to advanced 'World of Work' bulletin board using newspapers and photographs. Also reference the tourist album project (brochures, maps, newspapers, magazines, internet sources) as an example of printed text used for integrated skills across age groups. Keep the focus on how task demands—not text difficulty—shift across levels.

title: Risks of Authentic Materials and How to Manage Them
brief: Address the two main risks the source identifies: cultural load and difficulty. On cultural load, draw on the source's point that materials should reflect language learners are most likely to hear and use in their environment, and that listening texts can include native and non-native English likely to be used in the learners' context—implying that culturally distant material may not serve all learners equally. On difficulty, use the source's listed challenges for realia: materials can be a distraction if not carefully integrated into the lesson, may require changes in curriculum and extra planning, and may need alternative forms of assessment for task-oriented activities. Present the source's management strategies: choosing materials available locally; ensuring good quality of print, sound, or image; matching materials to learner age and interest; and designing tasks that allow learners to get as much information as they can from what they do understand rather than requiring full comprehension.

title: Selecting and Evaluating Authentic Materials: A Practical Checklist
brief: Synthesise the source's guidelines for choosing authentic materials into a practical decision-making framework teachers can apply before bringing any item into the classroom. Cover all six criteria listed in the source: the material is appropriate for the learner age group in terms of interest and language proficiency; it contains examples of the lesson point; it is in a style of English learners are likely to hear and use; it is available locally, on the internet, or has been collected by the teacher; it is of good quality in print, sound, or image; and it can be used for authentic-like tasks or activities. Reinforce each criterion with a brief illustrative example drawn from elsewhere in the source—for instance, the adult job-seekers unit where community newspapers were used as extensive reading because the topic matched learners' survival needs. End by connecting the checklist back to the unit's central idea: a well-chosen authentic material paired with a well-designed task is more valuable than a difficult text used without adaptation.
